personal_introduction.title: Introduce yourself
personal_introduction.prompt: Please introduce yourself. For example, you could talk about one of the following: your interests, your plans for future study, why you want to study abroad, why you need to learn English, why you chose this test.

read_aloud.title: Urban heat islands
read_aloud.text: Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Concrete and asphalt absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night, while the lack of vegetation reduces natural cooling. Planting trees and installing reflective roofs are two practical ways to reduce this effect.

read_aloud.title: The printing press
read_aloud.text: The invention of the printing press in the fifteenth century transformed the way knowledge was shared. Books, which had previously been copied by hand, could suddenly be produced quickly and cheaply. As a result, literacy rates rose across Europe, and new ideas in science and religion spread far beyond the universities and monasteries.

read_aloud.title: Sleep and memory
read_aloud.text: Research suggests that sleep plays a crucial role in consolidating memories. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay experiences from the day, strengthening the neural connections associated with new information. Students who sacrifice sleep to study late into the night may therefore remember less than those who rest properly.

read_aloud.title: Coral reefs
read_aloud.text: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support about a quarter of all marine species. These fragile ecosystems are threatened by rising sea temperatures, pollution and overfishing, and scientists warn that many reefs could disappear within a few decades.

read_aloud.title: Remote work
read_aloud.text: The shift towards remote work has changed the relationship between employers and employees. Many workers value the flexibility of choosing where they work, while managers have had to develop new methods of measuring productivity. Some companies now combine office and home working in a hybrid arrangement.

read_aloud.title: Volcanic islands
read_aloud.text: Many of the world's islands were formed by volcanic activity beneath the ocean. As lava erupts from the sea floor, it cools and hardens, gradually building a mountain that may eventually rise above the surface. Over thousands of years, wind and rain break down the rock into fertile soil, allowing plants and animals to settle.

read_aloud.title: Learning a language
read_aloud.text: Learning a new language takes patience and regular practice. Experts recommend studying for short periods every day rather than for several hours once a week, because frequent review helps the brain store new vocabulary more effectively.

read_aloud.title: The history of maps
read_aloud.text: Early maps were often more symbolic than accurate, reflecting the beliefs and priorities of the societies that produced them. It was only with the development of precise surveying instruments and, later, satellite imaging that cartographers could represent the shape of continents with remarkable precision.

read_aloud.title: Electric vehicles
read_aloud.text: Sales of electric vehicles have increased rapidly in recent years, encouraged by falling battery prices and government incentives. However, the expansion of charging networks has not always kept pace with demand, particularly in rural areas where drivers often travel long distances.

read_aloud.title: Museums online
read_aloud.text: Many museums now offer virtual tours that allow visitors to explore their collections from home. These online exhibitions have attracted new audiences who might never travel to the galleries themselves.

read_aloud.title: Biodiversity
read_aloud.text: Biodiversity refers to the variety of living organisms within a particular habitat or across the entire planet. Ecosystems with greater biodiversity tend to be more resilient, because the loss of one species is less likely to disrupt the functions on which the whole community depends.

read_aloud.title: Student budgets
read_aloud.text: For many students, university is the first time they must manage their own finances. Creating a simple monthly budget, tracking everyday spending and avoiding unnecessary debt can prevent considerable stress later in the academic year.

retell_lecture.title: Why bees matter
retell_lecture.transcript: Today I want to talk about why bees are so important. Around three quarters of the crops we grow for food depend, at least partly, on pollinators, and bees are the most efficient of them. When a bee visits a flower to collect nectar, pollen sticks to its body and is carried to the next flower, allowing the plant to reproduce. Unfortunately, bee populations have declined dramatically in many countries. Researchers point to three main causes: the widespread use of pesticides, the loss of wild flowers due to intensive farming, and diseases spread by parasites. If this decline continues, food prices could rise and our diets could become far less varied. The good news is that solutions exist. Farmers can plant strips of wild flowers alongside fields, governments can restrict the most harmful pesticides, and even individuals can help by growing bee-friendly plants in their gardens.

key_points.label: bees are vital pollinators for most food crops
how pollination works (pollen carried between flowers)
bee populations are declining
causes: pesticides, habitat loss, disease
consequences: higher food prices, less varied diets
solutions: wildflower strips, regulation, gardens

retell_lecture.title: The history of money
retell_lecture.transcript: Money, as we know it, is a relatively recent invention. For thousands of years, people relied on barter, directly exchanging goods such as grain for livestock. The problem with barter is that it requires what economists call a double coincidence of wants: you must find someone who has what you want and who also wants what you have. To solve this, societies began using commodity money, such as shells, salt, and later precious metals like gold and silver. Coins appeared in the kingdom of Lydia around the seventh century BC, and paper money was first widely used in China. Today, most money exists only as digital records in bank computers, and the value of a currency depends not on metal, but on trust in the government that issues it.

key_points.label: before money people used barter
barter needs a double coincidence of wants
commodity money: shells, salt, gold and silver
coins from Lydia, paper money from China
today money is mostly digital and based on trust

retell_lecture.title: Urban vertical farming
retell_lecture.transcript: Vertical farming means growing crops in stacked layers, usually indoors, under artificial light. Supporters argue that it could transform food production in crowded cities. Because the environment is fully controlled, crops can be harvested all year round, pesticides are rarely needed, and some systems use up to ninety percent less water than traditional agriculture. Food can also be grown close to consumers, which reduces transport emissions. However, the approach has serious drawbacks. The electricity needed for lighting and climate control is expensive, and unless it comes from renewable sources, the carbon footprint can actually be higher than that of conventional farms. At present, vertical farms are profitable mainly for leafy greens and herbs, not for staple crops like wheat or rice. So, while promising, vertical farming is likely to complement rather than replace traditional agriculture.

key_points.label: definition: crops grown indoors in stacked layers
advantages: year-round harvests, fewer pesticides, much less water
grown near consumers so lower transport emissions
drawback: high electricity cost and possible high carbon footprint
only profitable for leafy greens, not staples
conclusion: complement, not replace, traditional farming

retell_lecture.title: The science of habits
retell_lecture.transcript: Why are habits so hard to change? Neuroscientists explain that when we repeat an action in the same context, control gradually shifts from the decision-making parts of the brain to more automatic regions. That is efficient, because it frees up mental energy, but it also means habits run without our conscious attention. Research suggests that willpower alone is a poor tool for changing them. A more effective strategy is to change the environment: removing the cues that trigger an unwanted habit, and making the desired behaviour easier. For example, people who want to eat more healthily are far more successful when they simply stop keeping snacks at home. It typically takes around two months, not three weeks as is often claimed, for a new behaviour to become automatic.

key_points.label: repetition makes behaviour automatic in the brain
habits save mental energy but bypass conscious attention
willpower alone is ineffective
change the environment: remove cues, make good behaviour easy
example: not keeping snacks at home
about two months to form a habit, not three weeks

retell_lecture.title: Ocean currents
retell_lecture.transcript: Ocean currents act like a global conveyor belt, moving heat from the equator towards the poles. Surface currents are driven mainly by wind, while deep currents are driven by differences in temperature and salinity. In the North Atlantic, warm salty water travels north, cools, becomes denser and sinks, pulling more warm water behind it. This circulation is one reason why western Europe has milder winters than parts of Canada at the same latitude. Scientists are concerned that melting ice in Greenland is adding fresh water to the North Atlantic, which makes the surface water less dense and could slow the entire system. A significant slowdown could bring colder winters to Europe and change rainfall patterns in the tropics.

key_points.label: currents carry heat from equator to poles
surface currents driven by wind; deep currents by temperature and salinity
warm water sinks in the North Atlantic and drives circulation
gives western Europe milder winters
melting Greenland ice could slow the system
consequences: colder European winters, changed tropical rainfall

retell_lecture.title: Behavioural economics
retell_lecture.transcript: Traditional economics assumes that people make rational decisions to maximise their own benefit. Behavioural economics challenges this idea by showing that our choices are shaped by predictable biases. One example is loss aversion: losing fifty dollars feels roughly twice as painful as gaining fifty dollars feels good. Another is the default effect. When countries changed organ donation from an opt-in to an opt-out system, registration rates rose dramatically, even though people were free to choose either way. Governments now use these insights, sometimes called nudges, to encourage behaviour such as saving for retirement, without restricting anyone's freedom.

key_points.label: traditional economics assumes rational decisions
behavioural economics shows predictable biases
loss aversion: losses hurt about twice as much as gains
default effect: opt-out organ donation raised registration
governments use nudges, e.g. retirement saving

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Honestly, I'm worried about our group project. We're halfway through the semester and we still haven't agreed on a research question. Every meeting turns into a debate and nothing gets decided.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: I agree that it's frustrating, but I think the real problem is communication. Half of us don't read the group chat, so we keep repeating the same discussions. Maybe we should use a shared document where every decision is written down.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: A shared document is a good idea, but we also need someone to lead. I'd suggest we vote on a coordinator who sets deadlines. And if we still can't choose a question by Friday, we should ask the tutor for guidance during office hours.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That sounds reasonable. I'd be happy if Priya coordinated, actually. Let's set up the document tonight and try to finalise the question before Friday.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Fine by me. I'll create the document and share the link with everyone.

key_points.label: Maya: worried the group hasn't agreed on a research question; meetings become debates
Leo: the real problem is communication; suggests a shared document
Priya: need a coordinator/leader with deadlines; ask the tutor if stuck
outcome: Priya coordinates, Leo creates the document, decide by Friday

turns.speaker: Dr Chen
turns.text: The faculty is considering moving first-year lectures online permanently. I'd like to hear your views before the committee meets.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Personally, I'd welcome it. I work part-time, and recorded lectures let me study when it suits me. I can also pause and rewatch difficult sections, which really helps with technical subjects.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: I see the benefits, but I think first-year students especially need face-to-face contact. When I started university, the lectures were where I met people and felt part of a community. Online, it's easy to fall behind without anyone noticing.

turns.speaker: Dr Chen
turns.text: Both are fair points. One option is a blended model: recorded lectures for content, plus weekly in-person workshops for discussion and support.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: That would be a good compromise, as long as attendance at workshops is encouraged.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: I'd support that too, provided the workshops are offered at a few different times.

key_points.label: Dr Chen: faculty considering moving first-year lectures online; wants student views
Sam: supports online — flexibility for part-time work, can pause and rewatch
Aisha: first-years need face-to-face contact and community; risk of falling behind
Dr Chen proposes a blended model with weekly workshops; both students agree with conditions

turns.speaker: Professor Lee
turns.text: The library committee wants to know whether students would prefer the library to open twenty-four hours a day during exam periods. It would mean reducing evening hours during the rest of the year to cover staff costs.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: I'd definitely support it. Before exams the library is so crowded in the evenings that people can't find a seat. If it were open all night, students could spread out their study time.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: I'm not convinced. I worry it would encourage people to stay up all night, which isn't healthy. And cutting evening hours for the rest of the year would hurt part-time students who can only come after work.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee
turns.text: Those are both important concerns. What if we opened twenty-four hours only for the final two weeks before exams, and kept normal evening hours otherwise, funding it from the student services budget?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That would be fine with me.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: I could accept that, as long as the library also promotes healthy study habits during that time.

key_points.label: Professor Lee: committee asks about 24-hour opening in exams, funded by cutting evening hours
Nadia: supports it because the library is overcrowded before exams
Tom: worried about health and about part-time students losing evening hours
compromise: 24 hours only in the final two weeks, normal hours otherwise; both agree

turns.speaker: Dr Patel
turns.text: The department is writing a policy on AI writing tools. I'd like to hear how you think students should be allowed to use them in assignments.

turns.speaker: Kai
turns.text: I think they should be allowed for brainstorming and checking grammar. Banning them completely isn't realistic, and employers will expect us to know how to use them.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: I agree they're useful, but I'm worried about fairness. If some students use AI to write whole essays, the marks won't reflect real understanding. I'd want clear rules and some assessments done in class.

turns.speaker: Dr Patel
turns.text: So perhaps students could use AI for planning and editing, but must declare how they used it, and we add a short in-class written component to each module.

turns.speaker: Kai
turns.text: Declaring it seems reasonable.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Yes, and the in-class component would address my concern about fairness.

key_points.label: Dr Patel: department writing a policy on AI tools in assignments
Kai: allow AI for brainstorming and grammar; banning is unrealistic; employers expect it
Sofia: worried about fairness and real understanding; wants clear rules and in-class assessment
outcome: allowed for planning/editing with declaration plus in-class component; both agree
